stops.name: Solesmes, the town of the North
stops.campa: In Solesmes, a little town of the Cambrésis twenty kilometres east of Cambrai, François Alexandre Nicolas Chéri Delsarte is born on the nineteenth of November 1811. The father is an inventor whose contrivances devour the family's money; the mother comes of a better house and watches the fortune drain into failed devices. Into poverty the child is born who will one day chart the whole grammar of the human body. The flat wet fields of the North, the grey light, the hunger already in the house: these are his first teachers of what a body does under want.

stops.name: The road to Paris, the mother's flight
stops.campa: The father's inventions have ruined the house. The mother, of the wealthier line, will not sink with it; she leaves her husband and turns toward Paris to find work, taking the two eldest, François and his brother Louis, and leaving the two youngest with a grandmother. Along the winter roads out of the North the small family goes south toward the capital. It is the great division of the boy's life: the household broken, the road opening, the city ahead that will keep him and kill nearly everyone he brings to it.

stops.name: Paris, the death of mother and brother
stops.campa: In Paris the plan collapses into grief. The mother sickens and dies; the brother Louis dies after her. The boy is left alone in the enormous city, a child of nine or ten with no house and no protector. The tradition keeps the legend darker still: the brother frozen to death, held against François in the cold. Whether fever or frost took Louis, the fact that shapes everything is the same: the small warm body going cold in his arms, and the survivor turned forever toward the question of what the living body shows and what the dying body ceases to show.

stops.name: Paris, apprenticed to the porcelain painter
stops.campa: In 1822 François is bound apprentice to a porcelain painter of Paris. He learns the fine steady hand, the placing of a line, the reading of a face onto a plate: a first schooling of the eye in the exact registering of form. But music pulls harder than porcelain. The boy sings; he cannot stop singing; and the apprenticeship to the brush becomes the reluctant antechamber to the apprenticeship to the voice. Already the double gift is in him: the painter's eye that will one day map the body, and the singer's ear that the Conservatoire will ruin.
stops.quote: In 1822, François was apprenticed to a porcelain painter of Paris, but, yielding to a taste and aptitude for music, in the year 1825, he sought and obtained admission to the Conservatory as a pensioner.
stops.quote_source: Biographical note, Delsarte System of Oratory, tr. Frances A. Shaw

stops.name: Paris, the starving apprentice and Bambini
stops.campa: The apprentice years are years of hunger; the orphan lives on almost nothing, and the tradition tells of a body pushed to the edge of poisoning by what a starving boy will eat. Into this a deliverer comes: a music professor named Bambini hears the boy sing, recognises the instrument, and opens the way to the Conservatoire. The child who watched his brother die and painted faces onto porcelain to eat is lifted, by an ear that will not let his voice be lost, toward the school that will lose it for him.

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris, admission as pensioner
stops.campa: In 1825 Delsarte is admitted to the Paris Conservatoire as a pensioner, placed in the vocal classes. He enters with a true tenor and a hunger to be a great singer. Around him the reigning method is taught by rote and fashion: the forcing of the voice, the borrowed gesture, the artificial style of the age. He obeys the masters. Obeying them, he is destroyed. The very institution meant to make him a singer sets in motion the wound that will unmake the singer and make, in his place, the first law-giver of expression.
stops.quote: He had been placed in the vocal classes, and in consequence of faults in method and direction, he lost his voice.
stops.quote_source: Biographical note, Delsarte System of Oratory, tr. Frances A. Shaw

stops.name: Conservatoire de Paris, the voice breaks
stops.campa: The wound comes due. By the close of the 1820s the forced method has broken the instrument; the tenor is left with a voice ruined by bad teaching, inconsolable, his singer's career wrecked before it began. He will curse the arbitrary, unreasoning schooling of the Conservatoire to the end of his life. Yet from the ashes rises the vow that founds a science: if the masters cannot say WHY the voice is placed thus and the gesture made so, he will find the law himself. The wound turns the singer into a scientist of expression.
stops.quote: He was inconsolable, but, without making light of his sorrow, we may count that loss happy, which gave the world its first law-giver in the art of oratory.
stops.quote_source: Biographical note, Delsarte System of Oratory, tr. Frances A. Shaw

stops.name: Opéra-Comique, the singer with the ruined instrument
stops.campa: For a season Delsarte sings tenor at the Opéra-Comique, choosing his parts to spare the maimed voice, leaning already on the ACTING more than the tone, on the truth of the gesture more than the height of the note. He learns on the boards what the classes never taught: that an audience is moved less by the sound than by its manner, that a true attitude of the body persuades where a forced high note only astonishes. The failed singer is already, on stage, becoming the master of expression.
stops.quote: It is not what we say that persuades, but the manner of saying it.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory

stops.name: Jardin des Tuileries, the nurse and the child's thumb
stops.campa: In the Tuileries garden Delsarte watches the nurses and their charges for hours, week upon week, reading the language the body speaks before it knows it speaks. He marks a law in the smallest sign: as love wakes in an infant the fingers loosen and open, and when the true mother clasps the child the thumb springs wide from the hand, while the hired nurse never draws it so. From such minute and patient reading the whole doctrine grows: that every inner state has its outward sign, that gesture never lies, that the body has a grammar as fixed as speech.
stops.quote: Gesture is the direct agent of the heart, the interpreter of speech. It is elliptical discourse.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, address before the Philotechnic Society (Sorbonne), in Delsarte System of Oratory

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Rosine Andrien
stops.campa: On the fourth of June 1833 Delsarte marries Rosine Charlotte Andrien, a virtuoso pianist and teacher of solfège at the Conservatoire, of the house of Philippy de Bucelly d'Estrées. She becomes the keeper of the work he will never publish, the accompanist of his salons, the mother of his seven children. Through this marriage and his own sister's line he is bound to music's future: his sister Aimée is mother of Georges Bizet, so the maker of Carmen is the master of expression's own nephew. In 1833 too he prints his first treatise on singing.

stops.name: Hôpitaux de Paris, the wards of the dying
stops.campa: Delsarte goes into the hospital wards to watch the sick and the dying. He learns anatomy, takes courses in medicine, stands by beds to see how the failing body sheds its gestures: which sign goes first, which holds to the last breath. Here he grounds the science: not fancy but observation, the law read off the living and the perishing frame. He will say to depend on inspiration alone is as foolish as waiting for a shipwreck to learn to swim; the swimmer, and the actor, must know the law before the crisis.
stops.quote: To depend entirely upon inspiration is as bad as waiting for a shipwreck to learn how to swim.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, attributed, in Rick On Theater / Delsartean tradition

stops.name: The asylums and the graveside, the mad and the grieving
stops.campa: Into the asylums Delsarte goes to read the gestures of the mad, where the mask is torn off and the body speaks without governor; and to the cemeteries, to watch the grieving at open graves, where sorrow moves the frame past all pretence. In parks, cafés, churches, mortuaries, the scenes of disaster, he stations himself wherever feeling seizes the body and writes its sign plainly. From the whole reeling census of Paris he distils the constant: the same emotion draws the same gesture in every frame, and the correspondence can be charted.
